name: New Culture Movement
info: The New Culture Movement was a progressive sociopolitical movement in China in the 1910s and 1920s, in which scholars around the magazine New Youth criticised Confucian tradition and urged a vernacular literature, science and democracy.

facts.where: China, centred on Beijing, home of Peking University and Tsinghua University, and on Shanghai, with its flourishing publishing sector; some of its writers had first gathered in Tokyo
facts.period: The Tiger published in Tokyo 1914–1915; New Youth founded 1915; Hu Shih's literary reform essay January 1917; May Fourth protest 1919; the movement split over politics from 1919; overwhelmed by the anti-imperialist and populist violence of the mid-1920s
facts.figures: Chen Duxiu, founder of New Youth; Cai Yuanpei, chancellor of Peking University; Hu Shih, leader of the vernacular faction; Li Dazhao, librarian and editor; Lu Xun, author of Diary of a Madman; Gu Jiegang, historian of the Doubting Antiquity School; Chen Hengzhe, Bing Xin and Zhou Zuoren
facts.outcome: the written vernacular spread and a new literature appeared, while the movement divided: Hu Shih and the liberals returned to scholarship, and Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao took part in founding the Chinese Communist Party

t: The movement was launched by the writers of New Youth, who blamed Confucian culture for China's weakness and called for “Mr. Science” and “Mr. Democracy” in its place.
Hu Shih's argument that “a dead language cannot produce a living literature” led to the written vernacular, baihuawen, replacing Literary Chinese in literature.
The protest of 4 May 1919 turned a cultural movement into a political one, and its leaders then split: Hu Shih urged a return to study, while Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao turned to organised politics.
dyk: The first vernacular Chinese fiction was Chen Hengzhe's short story One Day, published in 1917, a year before Lu Xun's Diary of a Madman, which has often been incorrectly credited as the first.
ev: Zhang Shizhao founds the political magazine The Tiger in Tokyo; it runs until October 1915
Chen Duxiu founds the Youth Magazine, later retitled New Youth, marking the beginning of the movement
Hu Shih publishes Preliminary Discussion on Literary Reform in New Youth, urging writers not to imitate the ancients
Lu Xun publishes Diary of a Madman, which implies that China's traditional culture was mentally cannibalistic
Students in Beijing protest the transfer of German rights over Jiaozhou Bay to Japan, and the movement becomes political
The death of the student Li Chao becomes a rallying cry for anti-feudal and feminist agitation
New Culture reformers welcome Margaret Sanger's visit to China, and Hu Shih translates her speech on birth control
Rabindranath Tagore lectures in China and warns that it could encounter trouble by integrating too much progressive and foreign thought

sections.background:
After the 1911 Revolution, Yuan Shikai ended the second revolution of the summer of 1913 and forced many intellectuals into exile, some to Tokyo and others to Shanghai. In Tokyo in May 1914 Zhang Shizhao founded the political magazine The Tiger, which ran only until October 1915 but was one of the most influential political journals in China of its time. Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao contributed to it, and its writers grappled with how underlying cultural values and beliefs shape politics, a question that became important in the movement.

Yuan Shikai, who inherited part of the Qing dynasty military after its collapse in 1911, tried to establish order and unity but failed to protect China against Japan, and failed in an attempt to have himself declared emperor. In 1915 the Twenty-One Demands were issued, and six months later it became evident that Yuan intended to restore the imperial system. When he died in June 1916 the collapse of the traditional order seemed complete, and the search for a replacement went deeper than the changes of the previous generations, which had brought new institutions and new political forms.

The movement arose out of disillusionment with traditional Chinese culture following the failure of the Republic of China to address China's problems.
sections.aims:
The movement criticised many aspects of traditional Chinese society and favoured new formulations of Chinese culture informed by modern ideals of mass political participation. Its participants promoted a new society of unconstrained individuals rather than the traditional Confucian system. Chen Duxiu called for “Mr. Confucius” to be replaced by “Mr. Science” and “Mr. Democracy”, the two symbols of the movement.

Among its major positions were vernacular writing instead of classical literature, with Hu Shih's saying “Speak in the language of the time in which you live”; the emancipation of women; and the view that China is a nation among nations rather than a uniquely Confucian culture. It also promoted democratic and egalitarian values, a national orientation to the future rather than the past, and the re-examination of Confucian texts and ancient classics with modern textual and critical methods, known as the Doubting Antiquity School.

In the movement's view, Confucian morality repressed the universal and natural experience of sexuality, which they believed was best considered in scientific terms. Cai Yuanpei contended that divine authorities and superstitions should be overthrown, while seeing in religious aesthetics a potential for achieving transcendence through the appreciation of beauty.
sections.events:
In 1915 Chen Duxiu founded the Youth Magazine, later retitled New Youth. It began as a small operation but soon became much more influential than The Tiger had been. In 1917 Chen Duxiu and Zhang Shizhao moved to Beijing University, where they met the others who made up the movement's community. In January 1917 Hu Shih published Preliminary Discussion on Literary Reform in New Youth, with the guideline “Do not imitate the ancients”, and on 18 April 1918 he followed it with Constructive Literary Revolution – A Literature of National Speech.

On 4 May 1919 students in Beijing aligned with the movement protested at the transfer of German rights over Jiaozhou Bay to Imperial Japan rather than China at the Paris Peace Conference, which turned a cultural movement into a political one. When Cai Yuanpei resigned as principal of Beijing University on 9 May 1919 there was an uproar in the media across the country. The demonstrations first united the leaders, but they then fell out over the role of politics.

On 16 August 1919 the student Li Chao died of tuberculosis in poverty, after being cut off from her family's wealth for refusing a forced marriage and insisting on higher education. The publication of her private letters made her a martyr among radical students, and a memorial service on 30 November 1919 was held at the Women's Higher Normal School before thousands of guests.
sections.people:
The founders clustered at Peking University, where they joined the chancellor Cai Yuanpei. Chen Duxiu was Dean of the School of Arts and Letters and founder of New Youth, Li Dazhao was librarian, and Hu Shih was a leading figure in the literary revolution; the philosopher Liang Shuming and the historian Gu Jiegang were among the others. Many were classically educated. Li Dazhao campaigned for a new culture, opposed the enshrinement of Confucianism in China's constitution and wrote articles promoting Western civilisation, constitutional rule and democracy.

Hu Shih was considered the leader of the vernacular faction and used the textual study of Dream of the Red Chamber and other vernacular fiction as a basis for a national language. Scholars such as Zhao Yuanren began studying the varieties of Chinese with the tools of foreign linguistics. Lu Xun's essays and short fiction created a sensation: Diary of a Madman implied that China's traditional culture was mentally cannibalistic, and The True Story of Ah Q showed typical Chinese people as weak and self-deceiving. Mao Dun, Lao She and Bing Xin also published their first works in these years, and the movement promoted women writers.

Foreign thinkers mattered too. John Dewey arrived in 1919 and lectured for a year, and Bertrand Russell lectured widely to warm crowds. Cai Yuanpei, Li Shizeng and Wu Zhihui developed a Chinese variety of anarchism.
sections.outcomes:
The written vernacular was one outcome. In theory it allowed people with little education to read texts, articles and books, though the new vernacular included many foreign words and Japanese neologisms, which made it difficult for many to read. Journalism was modernised in the 1920s: editors and journalists became professionals, and the main Shanghai papers such as Shenbao moved away from the advocacy journalism of the 1911 period. Education was high on the agenda. Cai Yuanpei headed a New Education Society, and university students joined the Mass Education Movement of James Yen and Tao Xingzhi, which promoted literacy.

After May 1919 Hu Shih, Cai Yuanpei and other liberals urged demonstrating students to return to the classroom. Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao, frustrated with the inadequacy of cultural change, urged more radical political action and used their posts to organise Marxist study groups and the first meeting of the Chinese Communist Party. Li called for “fundamental solutions”; Hu answered with a call for “more study of questions, less study of isms”. Their younger followers included Mao Zedong. Gu Jiegang, who had studied the New History at Columbia University, applied it to classical Chinese texts in the Doubting Antiquity Movement.

New Culture intellectuals had advocated and debated a wide range of cosmopolitan solutions, including science, technology, individualism, music and democracy, and left to the future the question of what organisation or political power could carry them out. The anti-imperialist and populist violence of the mid-1920s soon overwhelmed their intellectual inquiry and culture.
sections.legacy:
Historians have judged the movement differently. Orthodox historians viewed it as a revolutionary break with feudal thought and the seedbed of the leaders who created the Chinese Communist Party and the People's Republic of China in 1949. Mao Zedong wrote that the May 4th Movement “marked a new stage in China's bourgeois-democratic revolution against imperialism and feudalism”. Historians in the west also saw a break between tradition and modernity, but Chinese and foreign historians now commonly argue that its changes had roots going back several generations and were an acceleration of earlier trends. Research also suggests that, besides radical Marxists, there were influential anarchists, conservatives, Christians and liberals.

Other historians argue that Mao's communist revolution betrayed the movement's spirit of independent expression and cosmopolitanism rather than fulfilling it. Yu Yingshi defended Confucian thought against the New Culture condemnation, reasoning that late imperial China had not been stagnant, irrational and isolated, and that late Qing thinkers were already drawing on the creative potential of Confucius. Xu Jilin, a Shanghai intellectual who reflects liberal voices, agreed that the movement was the root of the Communist Revolution but valued the outcome differently. He held that the cosmopolitan movement of the 1920s gave way to a “new age of nationalism”.

Many leaders of the Kuomintang, including Liao Zhongkai, Hu Hanmin and Dai Jitao, took part in the movement, and played a major role in restructuring the party along Soviet lines in 1922–1924.

summary: The New Culture Movement was a Chinese intellectual movement of the 1910s and 1920s, launched by the writers of New Youth, that attacked Confucian tradition and promoted the vernacular, science and democracy. After the May Fourth protest of 1919 its leaders divided over politics.
references: Tse-tsung Chow, The May Fourth Movement: Intellectual Revolution in Modern China (Harvard University Press, 2013)
Vera Schwarcz, The Chinese Enlightenment: Intellectuals and the Legacy of the May Fourth Movement of 1919 (University of California Press, 1986)
notes: Dates: the article gives only 'the 1910s and 1920s'. Start 1915 is the founding of the Youth Magazine ('marking the beginning'); end 1925 is approximate (circa) and rests on the article's 'mid-1920s' remark that violence overwhelmed the movement. The Tiger (1914) is placed in the background.
The article calls Li Chao's case 'reignited the movement'; I kept only the facts. Its closing claim that her death catalysed Communist laws is hedged ('It is believed') and was left out.
The article gives Lu Xun's Diary of a Madman as published 2 April 1918 and says The True Story of Ah Q 'was not published until 1921'; the sentence is garbled, so only the 1918 date was used.

Left out: Margaret Sanger detail beyond the event list, Tagore's views beyond one line, Li Shizeng and others' views on Social Darwinism and Nietzsche, the Crescent Moon Society, Yin Zizhong, Gu Jiegang's folk studies, Liang Shuming.
The sentence 'Hu Shih personally translated Sanger's speech' is in the event list; the article says the speech stressed birth control.
References left empty for the editor; the article's Bibliography has many works (Chow Tse-tsung, Schwarcz, Grieder, Meisner, Mitter, Spence).
